title: Still Operational
revision: Draft 1.0 — The Broken Link (first full draft)
paragraphs: At four forty-eight in the morning, Andrew discovered that Darius had prepared enough food to survive a very small siege.
The evidence occupied the common-room table in eight paper-wrapped parcels. Darius stood beside them with a pencil and a look of concentration usually reserved for recipes he was inventing.
“You're not taking all of that into combat,” Andrew said.
“Of course not,” Darius replied. “Some of it is for the journey.”

Nico appeared in the doorway, fastening the collar of his uniform with one hand and holding a piece of toast with the other. His curls had been crushed on one side by a night's sleep and remained rebelliously upright on the other.
“Is there coffee?” Nico asked.
“Good morning to you too,” Andrew said.
Nico regarded him. “I didn't want to waste valuable time saying things we both already know.”
“There's coffee,” Darius said. “It's not good coffee.”
“You made it. I trust you.”
“I didn't make the coffee.”
Nico stopped chewing. “Ah.”

Mara came in with a folded route card and a mug that looked as if she'd been drinking from it for an hour. Her hair was tied back tightly. She had already changed into her flight uniform, and there were dry mud marks at the cuffs from yesterday's reconnaissance around the depot.
“Fuel reserves checked. Northern corridor still open,” Mara said. “The first road gate expects us at five twenty.”
“Morning, Mara,” Andrew said.
“Good morning. The road gate expects us at five twenty.”
“See? She understands priorities,” Nico said.

Mara unfolded the card and held it toward Andrew. “The local detour report came in at three. No changes near the relay, but a bridge north of Hamburg is closed to heavy traffic. We'll use the western bypass.”
Andrew studied the route. The change would cost them a few minutes, maybe more if the checkpoint was busy. He'd rather lose the minutes than discover that a damaged bridge couldn't hold eight XR-17s.
“Use the bypass,” he said.
Mara looked faintly disappointed.
“You wanted an argument?” Andrew asked.
“Not especially.”
“You've been awake too long if you're disappointed by agreement.”
“I've been awake exactly as long as necessary.”
“That's what I tell Yelena,” Andrew said.
“Which is how I know it's a lie,” Yelena said from the doorway.

The medic carried a small case in one hand and an open notebook in the other. Her ash-brown braid lay over her shoulder. She didn't appear to have slept either, but Andrew knew better than to ask. She could become impressively offended by questions she asked everyone else.
“Nico, how many hours?” she said.
“Of what?”
“Sleep.”
“Ah. We are discussing personal matters before breakfast.”
“Four?”
“Five,” Nico said.
“Four and a half,” Andrew corrected.
Nico turned on him. “Traitor.”
“That's better than yesterday,” Yelena said, making a note.
“You're recording our failures now?” Nico asked.
“Only the ones with names.”
Juno arrived last, carrying a spanner he'd apparently forgotten to put down. The knuckles of his right hand were still marked with old grease. He spotted the breakfast parcels and picked one up.
“Is this mine?”
“Yes,” Darius said.
“Brilliant.”
“Did you sleep in the hangar again?” Mara asked.
“No, mate. I visited the hangar before coming here.”
“Your room is on the other side of the building,” Andrew said.
“Exactly. Had to make a proper trip of it.”
“Juno.”

“The bearing's perfect,” Juno said, anticipating the question. “Checked the housing, checked the grease, checked the travel. Nothing's shifted since yesterday. I'll run another diagnostic once the reactor's warm.”
“You already signed it off.”
“Yeah. And now I'm checking it again. That's the thing about repairs. You can be right twice.”
Sera entered quietly behind him and set her tablet on the table.
“You didn't check the left-rear thermal coupling,” she said.
Juno glanced back. “I did.”
“Three days ago.”
“Still counts.”
“Not for a two-hundred-kilometer drive.”
Juno stared at her for a moment. Then he picked up his parcel and sighed.
“Fine. I will check it again.”
Sera nodded. “Thank you.”
It occurred to Andrew that Sera could make Juno behave faster than any disciplinary action he'd ever tried. She rarely raised her voice and almost never wasted a word.
Akari pushed into the room with her camera hanging against her chest.
“Everybody,” she announced, “I have something important.”
“No,” Mara said.
“You haven't heard it yet.”
“I know.”
Akari turned to Andrew. “Can I get a picture at the gate? Just the mechs leaving together. It would look amazing if you all lined up properly.”
“We're not delaying a military operation for a photograph,” Andrew said.
“I only need ten seconds.”
Nico made a noise of outrage. “You said that yesterday.”
“Yesterday you moved!”
“Because you stepped on my foot!”
“I did not.”
“You nearly did,” Mara said.
Akari pointed at her. “You see? No actual injury. Perfectly safe.”
Andrew took one of the breakfast parcels and slipped it into his jacket. “Get a picture from the courtyard if you can do it without holding anyone up.”
Akari smiled immediately. “You are an excellent commander.”
“That's an opinion you can put in the report.”
She was already on her way to the door.

Darius watched her go, then passed the remaining food around. The little parcels contained bread rolls with cheese and something sweet that Andrew couldn't identify. Darius had written names on the wrappers, though Nico was already trying to negotiate a trade.
“Mine has the best one,” Nico told Juno.
“You haven't opened yours,” Juno replied.
“I can tell.”
“Then keep it.”
Nico frowned. “You're very difficult this morning.”

A few minutes later they crossed the courtyard, boots splashing through last night's rainwater. The converted depot looked almost sleepy beneath the low clouds: a kitchen window glowing yellow, the old administration wing, the patched hangar roof, a pair of utility trucks by the gate. It was hard to believe that eight combat mechs could live here without making the whole place seem more military than it did.
Then the hangar doors opened.

The XR-17s waited in two rows, their armored bodies crouched low between six articulated legs. Turrets faced the central aisle. The narrow, aggressive cockpits were dark until their pilots approached and the boarding systems woke in sequence.
Juno stopped beside his mech and ran his palm over the repaired front joint.
“Morning, sweetheart,” he murmured.
Nico heard him. “You talk to it like it's your girlfriend.”
“She's less argumentative than you.”
“It's because she can't answer.”
A maintenance display lit on the side of Juno's chassis. Sera looked at it, then at him.
“Left-rear thermal coupling.”
“Yep. Doing it now.”

Andrew headed for his own cockpit. The boarding ladder dropped from beneath the hull, and he climbed into the narrow compartment, pulled the harness across his shoulders and settled his boots onto the control rests.

His displays came alive in a familiar sequence. Reactor temperature. Joint alignment. Weapon safeties. Eight friendly identification markers appeared in the yard as the other pilots brought their systems online.
“Andrew to all units,” he said into the squad channel. “Radio check.”
“Mara. Clear.”
“Darius. Clear.”
“Juno. Clear, mate.”
“Akari. Perfectly clear.”
“Sera. Clear.”
“Yelena. Clear.”
“Nico. Testing. One, two, three. The handsome young communications officer wishes everyone a pleasant journey.”
“Nico,” Mara said, “clear your channel.”
“Technically it was already clear.”
Andrew suppressed a smile. Eight markers. Eight voices. Everyone here.

“Weapons safe through the civilian corridor,” he said. “Mara leads the route. Keep your spacing around settlements, and nobody passes a checkpoint without clearance. We'll meet the repair team at the northern depot.”
“Understood,” Mara said.

Andrew shifted the controls. His XR-17 lifted from its resting posture, all six legs extending together until the cockpit rose above the hangar floor. He felt the weight transfer through the chassis, the faint vibration as the reactor took the load.
Outside, Akari's cockpit canopy was still open. She had her camera raised.
“Hold still!” she shouted over the common channel.
“We're leaving,” Mara said.
“I'm taking it now.”
The eight mechs were halfway through arranging themselves into a column when Akari's camera clicked. It would be another terrible picture. Andrew hoped she kept it.
The depot gate slid aside.
“Move out,” Andrew said.
The column stepped through, turned north, and accelerated.

At first the mechs moved with the careful precision required by the roads near Celle. Their clawed feet landed on the paved shoulders beside the military lane, each step measured to avoid broken drainage covers and civilian cables. The six-legged gait was almost gentle at this speed. The pilots could have been escorting a parade.
The houses fell behind them.

Beyond the last checkpoint, the land opened into broad fields, low industrial buildings and service roads marked for military traffic. Mara took them onto a hardened strip running along the edge of an abandoned freight route.
“All units,” she said, “open section begins in two hundred meters. Maintain formation.”
The speed indicator climbed.

Andrew felt the XR-17 lengthen its stride. Its front legs reached forward, found ground and released almost before he registered the contact. The middle pair carried the weight through the turn of the gait; the rear pair drove the body onward. At speed, the movement became fluid enough that the cockpit scarcely pitched.
Forty miles an hour. Sixty. Eighty.
Juno's laughter came over the squad channel.
“That's more like it.”
“Save your enthusiasm for the inspection,” Sera said.
“I'm enthusiastic about that too.”

Andrew watched the speed touch ninety-seven, then settle. The XR-17s could sustain a hundred on open, favorable ground. Here the formation chose a little less to keep an easy margin between machines and preserve room to maneuver.
The fields passed in long, green-brown strips. A flock of birds lifted from a ditch, and Akari's mech shifted sideways to avoid the uneven ground. She did it without losing her place in line.
“That was a lovely turn,” Juno said.
“Thank you,” Akari replied. “You may compliment me again after the mission.”
“Didn't mean you. Meant the leg system.”
“You're impossible.”
“Put it in the report,” Juno said.

They slowed before the first occupied village. A faded school sign stood beside a row of houses with patched windows. On the square, traders had arranged jars, vegetables and homemade soap beneath an awning. A line of people waited outside a ration office. The eight XR-17s passed at a crawl.
A boy in a yellow coat waved both arms.
Akari raised her mech's right foreleg briefly.
“Akari,” Mara said, “watch your clearance.”
“Plenty of clearance.”
“The market stall disagrees.”
Akari lowered the leg. The boy laughed and kept waving.
Andrew saw a woman take the child's hand and pull him farther from the road. She didn't look angry. She just looked as if she'd already spent the morning being worried about other things.

At the next checkpoint, a column of civilian vehicles was waiting under a temporary roof of camouflage netting. Some had luggage tied to their roofs. Others carried mattresses, bicycles or plants in plastic buckets.
An elderly man sat on the edge of a truck bed, holding a cage covered with a towel. Whatever lived inside shifted when the XR-17s passed.
The checkpoint officer appeared on Andrew's forward display, helmet camera catching a tired face and a sleepless pair of eyes.
“Walker detachment?” the officer asked.
“That's us,” Andrew said. “Eight mechs, northbound to the Neumünster relay.”
“Your passage is cleared. Keep west after the next junction. Bridge crew's still working the eastern span.”
“Any changes up ahead?”
“Not on your assigned corridor. There's artillery farther north. Listen to the route channel if you want the depressing details.”
Andrew hesitated. “And the civilians?”
The officer glanced away from the camera. “Those who can go south are going south. Still got people coming north for work, if you can believe it.”
Andrew could.
The officer stepped aside, and the barrier lifted.

When the squad was clear, Mara switched them back to the military corridor. They accelerated again, though not as fast as before. A maintenance convoy occupied one lane, and beyond it crews were reinforcing a line of concrete barriers. Their bulldozer had lost a track and stood crooked beside the road.
Darius broke the quiet on the channel.
“Those people at the checkpoint have been waiting since before dawn,” he said.
“Probably longer,” Yelena replied.
“Do you think the old man had a cat?”
“In the cage?” Nico asked.
“It moved.”
“Could be a chicken,” Juno said.
“Not if Yelena has anything to say about it,” Akari replied.
Yelena paused. “A chicken is also a patient.”
Andrew smiled. The squad could find its way back to ordinary conversation almost anywhere. He wasn't sure whether it was a skill they'd learned or a habit they refused to give up.

North of Hamburg, the clouds lowered and the landscape changed. Defensive markers appeared beside the road, then concrete firing positions, then embankments built from earth and broken stone. The population was thinner here, though no less busy. Mechanics worked beneath vehicles. Uniformed volunteers carried cable drums. A group of children helped stack empty crates outside a clinic while a tired teacher tried to keep them away from the road.
On a rise to the east, Andrew could see an artillery battery adjusting its barrels.
The radio carried a request for replacement ammunition, followed by a reply too faint to make out.
“That's not our sector,” Mara said.
“I know,” Andrew replied.
A few moments later the ground gave a distant, hollow thud. The artillery line had fired.
Nico reduced the volume of the general traffic channel. “They've been busy.”
“Keep the local channel up,” Andrew said.
“Already is.”

Andrew checked the time. They'd covered most of the distance in a little over two hours, with the delays and slower sections accounting for as much of the journey as the open ground. Mara's estimate had been good.
The forward depot came into view shortly after eight.

It occupied the grounds of a former distribution center, surrounded by hurriedly built walls and an assortment of buildings that had not been designed to withstand a battle. One warehouse had lost half its roof. Workers had enclosed the loading docks with sandbags. A row of civilian vans waited behind concrete barriers.
There were fewer mechs here than Andrew expected.

The depot sentry cleared the gate for their eight XR-17s, then directed them to a hardened inspection pad. Andrew brought his mech down into a low waiting posture while the other seven took positions around the square.
“Don't block the medical entrance,” Mara said.
“Wasn't going to,” Nico replied.
“You're standing across it.”
“Ah.”
Nico shuffled his mech three meters to the side.

Andrew opened his canopy. Cool air washed across his face, carrying the smell of damp concrete and engine exhaust. He climbed down and found a woman in a faded orange work jacket waiting beneath the pad lights.
“Andrew Walker?” she asked.
“Yes.”
“Leonie Krüger. Communications maintenance.” She held out a gloved hand. “You're early.”
“We tried.”
“Good. I don't think this station has another afternoon to spare.”
Behind her, two small utility vans stood packed with replacement cable, tools and portable batteries. A young technician was checking a coil of wire, while an older driver studied a greasy map.
Leonie followed Andrew's glance. “That's Mika with the spare modules. Oskar drives the second van. Three technicians, two vans. We'd have come with half that if I thought I could get away with it.”
“What's failed?” Andrew asked.

“That depends on which piece of the relay you ask. The primary line started dropping packets two days ago. Last night the backup power feed became intermittent. We think water got into a coupling housing during the storm.”
“You think?” Mara asked as she climbed down from her own cockpit.
Leonie gave her a look. “If it were certain, I'd be standing at the relay with a replacement part instead of standing here explaining why we need an escort.”
Mara nodded. “Fair.”

A thin man in a stained field jacket emerged from the depot office. His sleeve carried a worn service insignia. He introduced himself as Sergeant Brandt and brought them inside to a map pinned over a table.

“Relay's here,” Brandt said, tapping a mark northeast of the depot. “The eastern bridge is underwater. Engineers closed it last night. West route goes through the old workshop ground and cuts back toward the relay after the drainage culvert.”
“Mara's route,” Andrew said.
Brandt looked at her. “Good choice. We used it for recovery traffic before the floods.”
“West watch?” Mara asked.
“Two observation posts, intermittent contact. One crew pulled back before dawn to support the northern batteries.”
“Which one?” Andrew asked.
Brandt pointed to the post overlooking the road's far side.
Andrew studied the map. That post would have watched the blind section.
“We requested coverage,” Mara said.
“Request reached us,” Brandt replied. “We can't give you people we don't have.”
He didn't offer a dramatic explanation. He simply moved his finger north.

“Two sectors have been asking for reinforcements since midnight. We're still holding here. My job is to make certain your technicians get through. Yours is to make certain the road stays open long enough to do it.”
Leonie leaned over the map. “And my job is to fix the relay before another convoy spends a night parked in the open.”
“Exactly,” Andrew said.

He asked Brandt for the latest patrol times. Mara compared them with the water report. Nico checked their short-range channels and arranged a backup set of coded light signals in case the local radios failed. Sera pulled up the forward observation feeds. Juno inspected the repaired joint on his own mech and checked the heat readings, ignoring Nico's commentary while he worked.
Yelena opened Leonie's medical case.
“You have dressings,” Yelena said.
“Yes.”
“Tourniquets?”
Leonie pointed to a side pocket.
“Good. Keep them where you can reach them.”
Mika, the young technician, watched her repack the case.
“Will we need those?” he asked.
“Hopefully not,” Yelena said.
He didn't look reassured.
She closed the case and handed it back. “That's why we're bringing them.”
Andrew returned to the map. The western route was marked in pencil, with the old workshop yard circled in blue.

“Here's the hardstand,” Mara said. “If anything goes wrong, the vans stop here. The culvert's three hundred meters of poor sightline. We keep the mechs on both sides of the road as far as the ground allows.”
“Can your machines move faster than ours?” Leonie asked.
“A little,” Juno said from the door.
“Don't,” Sera said without looking up.
Leonie raised an eyebrow.
“A hundred miles an hour on good ground,” Andrew explained. “We won't be doing anything close to that near your vans.”
“Wonderful,” Leonie said. “I had enough reasons to be nervous.”
Andrew smiled. “We'll keep you together.”
Brandt's desk radio crackled. A voice from a northern battery requested confirmation of a firing lane. Brandt answered in clipped German, then switched the set off again.
“Stay on your assigned route,” he told Andrew. “I can't spare another unit if you go looking for a bigger fight.”
“We aren't looking for one.”
Brandt glanced at the eight mechs outside. “Glad to hear it.”
Andrew signed the escort sheet, passed the final route confirmation to Mara and climbed back into his XR-17.
“Everyone ready?” he asked on the squad channel.
One by one, seven voices answered.
The two utility vans started their engines. Their brake lights glowed red against the wet loading docks.
“Escort formation,” Andrew said. “Let's go put the north back on the radio.”
